one_liner: Tiny interruptible SAX-style (callback) JSON parser and printer in C; its suite wins over nlohmann/json come from harness code.
what_it_does: Two files (json.c, json.h) give a streaming parser that you feed bytes or chunks of any size (json_parser_string/json_parser_char) and that calls one callback per event (object/array begin and end, key, string, int, float, true, false, null), plus a printer that turns the same events into compact or indented text through an output callback. There is no object model and no number conversion: numbers reach the callback as validated strings. An optional json_parser_dom helper builds a tree through three user callbacks. It is not a drop-in for nlohmann/json: you write the tree, the number conversion and the serialiser walk yourself.
how_it_is_fast: A hand-written table-driven state machine (derived from json.org's JSON_parser.c): each input byte goes through a 128-entry character-class table, a 37-state by 34-class transition table, a parallel buffer-policy table and a UTF-8 header/continuation table, with no backtracking and no number conversion. Parser state is a small struct (256-byte nesting stack, 4 KB value buffer by default; the suite's SAX statistics run peaked at 4,352 bytes). There is no SIMD or bulk scanning: string bytes are copied into the value buffer one at a time, and the printer calls the output callback once per string byte, so throughput lags RapidJSON-class parsers.
when_to_use: Input arrives in arbitrary chunks from a socket, pipe or serial line and you want to parse it incrementally with bounded state (no full-document buffer, about 4.3 KB of parser memory in the suite's SAX run).
Pass-through or reformatting tools (lint, pretty-print, filters) that must keep numbers verbatim: big integers and long decimals are handed over as strings, never rounded.
Number-heavy SAX workloads where YAJL is the incumbent: in the 2016 suite the SAX round-trip of canada.json took 14.7 ms vs YAJL 112.8 ms, and SAX statistics 11.5 vs 40.9 ms.

Small embedded or plain-C programs that want a dependency-free parser with optional nesting and size limits, custom allocators and optional C or # comments (jsonstat code-size binary 26,036 bytes vs 42,132 for nlohmann).
You already have your own tree type (GLib hash tables, an arena) and want the parser to fill it directly through callbacks.
when_not_to_use: You want a DOM or typed access like nlohmann/json: the suite's tree built through json_parser_dom parsed 1.48x slower than nlohmann v2.0.3 (107.2 vs 72.5 ms over three files) and far slower than cJSON (24.7 ms), udp/json-parser (47.3 ms) or RapidJSON (7.9 ms).

Raw parse throughput matters: the byte-at-a-time state machine has no SIMD; SAX statistics totalled 22.5 ms vs RapidJSON 6.3 ms, and on string-heavy files it lost to YAJL (citm_catalog 7.95 vs 4.74 ms, twitter 3.06 vs 1.71 ms).

Untrusted input where strict UTF-8 matters: the validator accepts overlong C0/C1 leaders, 5- and 6-byte forms (F8-FD) and code points above U+10FFFF, and \u0000 yields NUL bytes inside values (open issue #31).
Documents whose root is a scalar (allowed by RFC 7159/8259): the start state only accepts '{' or '[' (RFC 4627 behaviour).
Static linking into proprietary code: LGPL 2.1 or 3.0 only, and the repo carries no LICENSE file.

integration.form: source-drop (json.c + json.h; the Makefile also builds a static/shared lib and jsonlint on Linux/BSD)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; plain C using stdint.h, inline and // comments (C99 or C89 with extensions), with shims for MSVC before 2010; header has extern "C" guards for C++
integration.platforms: any (portable byte-wise C, no SIMD); the author recommends embedding the two files rather than using the build system on Windows or macOS
integration.thread_safety: not documented; by code reading all mutable state lives in caller-owned json_parser, json_printer and json_parser_dom structs and the lookup tables are only read, so one context per thread is independent

gotchas: Harness flaws behind the numbers (nativejson-benchmark src/tests/vincenthzlibjsontest.cpp, unchanged since 2016): tree_print ignores its print_func argument and always calls json_print_raw, so the Prettify row is compact output and void; it emits false and null as JSON strings, so citm_catalog and twitter Stringify output is wrong; numbers are formatted by harness sprintf and parsed by harness strtoll/atof; and the Parse row (the one libjson loses) includes the harness's grow-by-one realloc per appended element (334,389 allocations on canada.json vs 170,254 for nlohmann).

Conformance correction: sample/conformance.csv is stale. Harness fixes 274281a and 95936a1 (2016-09-10, a day after the sample run) give 34 of 34 parse validation and 9 of 9 strings; the remaining 8 of 66 double failures are harness strtoll saturating big integers at 9.2233720368547758e18, and all 10 of 27 round-trip failures are harness artifacts (false/null printed as strings, %.17g formatting). None is attributable to libjson's parser.

Security history: json_parser_dom's dom_push grew its stack by newsize bytes instead of elements (heap overflow past 1,024 nesting levels). The fix e03b4a9 was authored 2018-10-06 but only merged to master on 2024-04-27 (PR #27), so copies vendored before 2024 are vulnerable. Issues #31-#33 (2026-06-15: lax UTF-8, uint32 overflow in dom_push, stack[-1] write on direct API misuse) are open with no maintainer reply; json_parser_dom_callback also ignores dom_push's out-of-memory return.

API quirks: the README names json_printer_init/_pretty/_raw but the header exports json_print_init, json_print_pretty and json_print_raw; printer functions always return 0 and ignore the output callback's return value; json_parser_dom_init zeroes the struct before allocating, so custom allocators never apply to the initial 1,024-entry stack; nesting and size limits default to 0 (unlimited). Unrelated projects named libjson (SourceForge, xnacly) sit in the same category.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over cJSON, json.h or udp/json-parser only when you need a resumable, chunk-fed callback parser with constant memory and verbatim number strings; those siblings parse to a DOM 2-6x faster in the same suite. Compared with jsmn (also no number conversion), libjson keeps its own state across arbitrary chunk boundaries instead of needing the whole buffer and a token array; for raw speed use yyjson or simdjson.
verified_claims_summary: In nativejson-benchmark's 2016-09-09 sample run (Core i7-4980HQ, Apple clang 7.0, -O3 -march=native, libjson at bd0cad8 vs nlohmann/json v2.0.3), a harness tree printer calling libjson's json_print_raw stringified the three files in 68.8 ms vs 87.7 ms (about 1.28x, derived from page data) while writing false/null as strings, the Prettify win is void (no pretty-printing happened), and the Parse row that uses libjson's parser was 1.48x slower than nlohmann. libjson's own SAX rows have no nlohmann baseline; they beat YAJL on number-heavy canada.json and lose to it on the string-heavy files.
status_note: Low-activity but alive (PR merges in 2024-04 and 2026-05, last commit 2026-05-12) with three security issues from 2026-06 unanswered; LGPL-2.1-only OR LGPL-3.0-only per the file headers (no LICENSE file), small enough to vendor and audit, and kept with tier C because every row that beats nlohmann times buggy benchmark code.
